content: Care should be integrated throughout an individual’s life course, as it is fundamental to enhancing quality of life, well-being, comfort, and human dignity. It is also recognized as an effective, person-centered health service. The World Health Organization (WHO) emphasizes the need for universal health coverage to include the full spectrum of essential, high-quality health services, ranging from health promotion and prevention to treatment, rehabilitation, and palliative care across the life course. Palliative care is considered an essential component of comprehensive care for individuals living with HIV due to the diverse symptoms they may experience. Despite evidence showing that individuals with life-threatening illnesses often prefer to die at home, studies across 11 countries reveal that people living with HIV are more likely to die in hospitals compared to those with cancer. Health policies should be designed to respect and enable end-of-life care preferences. The essential medicines for palliative care are based on the 2019 WHO Model List of Essential Medicines, selected for their ability to alleviate the most common types of suffering among individuals with HIV and other serious illnesses. These medicines are chosen for their clinical effectiveness, safety, affordability, and accessibility. Morphine, in both oral fast-release and injectable forms, is indispensable for managing pain and refractory terminal dyspnea. However, regulatory barriers to accessing controlled medicines like morphine should not arise from efforts to prevent their misuse. The 2020 WHO guidelines on managing chronic pain in children affirm that access to pain management is a fundamental human right. Governments are obligated to ensure the availability of essential medicines, including opioid analgesics, as part of their core responsibilities under the right to health. In addition to pharmaceutical management, self-management strategies can empower individuals living with HIV, especially in contexts where stigma and barriers to clinical support persist. Systematic reviews have shown that self-management interventions, delivered online, in person, or in groups, can effectively alleviate pain and physical symptoms in people living with HIV. WHO recommends that all healthcare providers receive at least basic palliative care training, given the diverse range of professionals involved in care delivery, including community and primary care providers, pediatricians, and HIV specialists. Basic training should focus on competencies in assessing and relieving pain, managing physical symptoms, addressing mental distress such as anxiety and depression, and tackling social suffering, including stigma, abandonment, and poverty. Training should also emphasize empathetic and culturally sensitive communication, medical ethics, advance care planning, interdisciplinary teamwork, end-of-life care, bereavement support, and self-care. Curricula for such training are available, with basic training lasting 30–40 hours for primary care providers and intermediate-level training lasting 60–80 hours for specialists in fields such as HIV management, infectious diseases, oncology, and critical care. Palliative care services should be accessible at all levels of the healthcare system and in the home. Central-level hospitals caring for individuals with HIV should have dedicated palliative care teams, including doctors (preferably palliative care specialists), nurses, and social workers or psychologists, to provide inpatient and outpatient care and support clinicians at lower levels. District hospitals should have at least one doctor and nurse with basic palliative care training, along with a social worker, to deliver palliative care as an official responsibility. Primary healthcare centers should have at least one healthcare worker trained in basic palliative care to initiate and manage care for individuals with uncomplicated needs, continue care initiated in hospitals, and provide home visits when feasible. Community health workers can be trained to recognize uncontrolled suffering and communicate concerns to palliative care teams using mobile health technologies. Supervision by healthcare professionals is essential for community health workers providing palliative care. Person-centered HIV care delivered in the community by trained professionals can improve physical, mental, social, and spiritual well-being and enhance retention in care. Social support is a critical component of early palliative care consultations and should be accessible to anyone in need, particularly in cases of extreme poverty. Social support may include transport vouchers, cash payments, food packages, and other in-kind assistance, which should be funded through anti-poverty or social welfare programs rather than healthcare budgets. For children and adolescents living with HIV, access to antiretroviral therapy (ART) has improved their quality of life and developmental potential. However, service delivery platforms must address chronic comorbidities, disabilities, and developmental delays. Early childhood is a critical period for laying the foundation for lifelong health, well-being, and productivity. Children living with HIV face unique vulnerabilities, including being born prematurely or small for gestational age, experiencing severe infections, suboptimal nutrition, and being raised in challenging social environments. These factors can limit their developmental potential. Enabling children to achieve their full developmental potential is a human right and essential for sustainable development. WHO has developed guidelines to strengthen policies and programs for early childhood development, emphasizing the importance of nurturing care, which includes good health, adequate nutrition, safety, responsive caregiving, and opportunities for early learning. These efforts should begin during pregnancy and continue throughout the life course. Integrating a nurturing care approach into maternal, newborn, and child health services, as well as HIV prevention and care, can improve the quality of engagement between healthcare workers and caregivers. As children and adolescents with HIV age, comprehensive care remains critical. There is increasing recognition of the risk of chronic multisystem comorbidities and disabilities among children on ART. Adolescents with perinatally acquired HIV are particularly vulnerable to developmental delays, neurocognitive impairments, mental health disorders, and organ system morbidities, such as chronic lung, heart, and kidney diseases. Growth and bone density are also affected, with delayed ART initiation leading to stunted growth and reduced bone density, which increases fracture risk in adulthood. Surveillance and monitoring of growth and comorbidities are essential, particularly as newer ART regimens with fewer toxicities become available. Chronic lung disease associated with HIV is more commonly reported in low-income settings, likely due to risk factors such as recurrent infections, delayed ART initiation, household air pollution, malnutrition, and stunting. These factors can lead to reduced lung function and volume, which persist into adulthood. Addressing these issues requires early intervention and comprehensive care to mitigate long-term health impacts.
